teaser: It is past midnight in this painting, and the sun is already coming back.
review_notes:
Zorn returned to Mora for good in 1896 after about eight years based in Paris; the painting was made in the hamlet of Morkarlby in 1897 at the suggestion of Prince Eugen: check.
Zorn wrote that he had revived the maypole custom in Morkarlby and given the village its pole: check his memoirs.
The four-color 'Zorn palette' (yellow ochre, vermilion, ivory black, white) is a widely repeated tradition; he did use other pigments at times, and the lesson says 'often'.
Zorn painted Grover Cleveland (1899) and William Howard Taft (1911) and etched Theodore Roosevelt (1905); the lesson says 'three American presidents sat for him' without specifying medium.
Fiddlers' contest founded 1906 at Gesunda near Mora.
The scene is read as dawn (rising sun gilding the gable and windows), following Zorn's own description: check.
The claim that his etchings once sold for more than Rembrandt's is often repeated: check.
Size 140 x 98 cm. The signature at lower right reads Zorn with a date (legible in the image as Zorn 97).

lesson.text: By 1897 Anders Zorn had everything a painter is supposed to want. He was thirty-seven. He had lived in Paris for years, his portraits of bankers and society ladies sold for huge sums, and America was calling. The year before, he had done something his clients found odd: he moved back to Mora, the farming parish in central Sweden where he was born.

He had left it as a poor boy. His mother worked in a brewery, his father was a German brewer he never met, and he grew up on his grandparents' farm. Now he came back wealthy, built a house, and set about painting his neighbors. This canvas, about 1.4 meters tall (4.5 feet), is the one he said held his deepest feeling.

The occasion is Midsummer, the biggest night of the Swedish year, in late June. A tall pole wrapped in leaves is raised, and then the village dances around it until morning. Zorn puts you right in the yard, at elbow height with the dancers. But where is the pole?
The whole party turns around one object, and Zorn has pushed it to the edge. Find the maypole.

spots.title: At the far edge
spots.text: A thin dark mast against the sky, with crossed arrows, two hanging wreaths and a flag at the tip. The star of the feast is a silhouette in the corner.

lesson.text: A more official painter would have centered that pole and arranged the villagers around it like a stage chorus. Zorn does the reverse. He fills the front with one spinning couple, cuts another off at the left edge, and lets the symbol shrink. You are not shown a custom. You are in the middle of the dance floor.
The pole may be there thanks to Zorn himself. He wrote that the custom had died out in this hamlet and that he revived it, paying for a new maypole. The painter was also the party's sponsor.

Then there is the light, which is strange once you think about it. The sky is pale and the grass is clearly green, yet no one casts a strong shadow. This far north, the Midsummer sun dips below the horizon for only a few hours and the night never turns black. And one building tells you what time it has become.

lesson.title: The hour and the hand
lesson.text: First the clock, then the way the paint is put down.

spots.title: Windows on fire
spots.text: The panes of the red house glow yellow, and its gable is warmer than everything around it. They are catching the first rays of sunrise. These people have danced all night.

spots.title: Two faces, close
spots.text: Her kerchief nearly covers her profile. He looks down, hat tipped, concentrating on his feet. Neither is posing. The red straps and sash are single unbroken strokes.

spots.title: A flash of white
spots.text: Her dark skirt swings out and a white underskirt shows for an instant. A few slashes of pale paint are enough to tell you how fast she is turning.

spots.title: Grass in a hurry
spots.text: The ground is long diagonal sweeps of green, ocher and brown, laid on wet and left alone. Up close it is nearly abstract.

lesson.text: Zorn paints fast so that the picture keeps the speed of what it shows. The brushstrokes turn with the dancers.

That speed was trained. In Paris he had watched the Impressionists, who painted outdoors with quick, visible touches to catch a passing light. He shared their appetite for the moment, though his color stayed earthier than theirs. He often worked with very few pigments: an ocher yellow, a red, black and white.

With black and white alone he could mix a gray that looks blue beside warm colors. Painters still call a set of just four tubes, yellow ocher, red, black and white, the Zorn palette, and use it as a training exercise.

Count the colors here and the claim holds up surprisingly well. White blouses, black skirts and hats, red straps and one red house, golden light. The greens of the grass are muted, close to olive. The restraint is what lets the small reds ring out across the yard, from the nearest sash to the far wall.

The picture also carried an argument. In the 1890s Sweden was industrializing and country people were leaving for cities and for America. Painters and writers answered with a wave of pride in rural life. Zorn's dancers wear the local dress of Mora, which he encouraged villagers to keep. Later he founded contests to save the old fiddle tunes.
Fame abroad never slowed. Three American presidents sat for him, and at one point his etchings fetched higher prices than Rembrandt's.

He could have lived anywhere. He kept choosing this yard, these log walls, this slope of grass at four in the morning. The painting now hangs in the national museum in Stockholm and has become, for many Swedes, simply what Midsummer looks like.

quiz.question: What had Zorn done the year before he painted this?
options: Moved back to his home parish of Mora
quiz.explanation: After years in Paris he returned to Mora in 1896.

quiz.question: Where does Zorn place the maypole?
options: It is not in the picture
At the far right edge, as a thin silhouette
quiz.explanation: The symbol of the feast is pushed to the edge while the dancers fill the front.

quiz.question: What do the glowing windows of the red house tell you?
options: The sun is rising after a night of dancing
Lamps have been lit for the evening
quiz.explanation: The panes catch the first rays of sunrise.

quiz.question: Which colors make up the so-called Zorn palette?
options: Yellow ocher, red, black and white
quiz.explanation: He often limited himself to those four.

quiz.question: Why is there so little shadow in the scene?
options: The northern summer night never gets fully dark
quiz.explanation: At Midsummer the sun dips below the horizon for only a few hours.

facts.text: Zorn grew up in a wealthy family of Stockholm bankers.
facts.explanation: He was raised on his grandparents' farm in Mora, the son of a brewery worker.

facts.text: Zorn wrote that he revived the maypole custom in the hamlet he painted.
facts.explanation: He said the tradition had died out there and he paid for a new pole.

facts.text: The scene takes place in the early afternoon.
facts.explanation: It is dawn: the first sun lights the windows after a night of dancing.
